fuentes/tratado-de-benegas/autor.texto: Governments of Buenos Aires and Santa Fe

fuentes/tratado-de-benegas/resumen.texto: Peace treaty signed on November 24, 1820 at the Benegas estancia, near San Nicolás de los Arroyos, between Buenos Aires and Santa Fe, with the mediation of Córdoba. It ended the war that followed Cepeda and bound the parties to convene a congress in Córdoba. In a separate agreement, Juan Manuel de Rosas undertook to hand over 25,000 head of cattle to Santa Fe as compensation for the war’s damages.

fuentes/tratado-de-benegas/por_que_impor.texto: It closed the war between Buenos Aires and Santa Fe of 1820 and separated Estanislao López from Francisco Ramírez, who continued the war and died in 1821.

fuentes/tratado-del-cuadrilatero/autor.texto: Governments of Buenos Aires, Santa Fe, Entre Ríos and Corrientes

fuentes/tratado-del-cuadrilatero/resumen.texto: Peace, friendship and alliance treaty signed in Santa Fe on January 25, 1822 by Buenos Aires, Santa Fe, Entre Ríos and Corrientes. The four provinces mutually guaranteed each other’s territory, left boundary questions for a future general congress, declared trade between them free and navigation in national ships free, and, following Buenos Aires, which had withdrawn from the congress that Bustos had convened in Córdoba, committed themselves to not joining a congress for now. Santa Fe was to withdraw its deputy from there.

fuentes/tratado-del-cuadrilatero/por_que.texto: It closed the cycle of Litoral wars that followed Cepeda and nullified the Córdoba congress of 1821, leaving national organization postponed until the Congress of 1824.

fuentes/ley-fundamental-1825/titulo.texto: Fundamental Law of the General Constituent Congress

fuentes/ley-fundamental-1825/autor.texto: General Constituent Congress of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata

fuentes/ley-fundamental-1825/resumen.texto: Law passed on January 23, 1825 by the Congress meeting in Buenos Aires. It declared the Congress constituent and the independence of the United Provinces. It established that each province would be governed by its own institutions until a constitution was enacted, and that the constitution would be submitted to the provinces’ acceptance before being promulgated. It provisionally entrusted the government of Buenos Aires with the national executive power over foreign relations.

fuentes/ley-fundamental-1825/por_que_imp.texto: It set the rule that the constitution depended on the consent of the provinces, which they invoked in 1826 to reject the unitary Constitution.

fuentes/ley-fundamental-1825/leer.0.titu.texto: Text in the Registro Nacional de las Provincias del Río de la Plata, on Wikisource

fuentes/tratado-con-gran-bretana-1825/ti.texto: Treaty of Friendship, Commerce and Navigation between the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata and Great Britain

fuentes/tratado-con-gran-bretana-1825/so.texto: Treaty signed by Manuel José García and Woodbine Parish

fuentes/tratado-con-gran-bretana-1825/re.texto: Treaty signed in Buenos Aires on February 2, 1825 by Manuel José García and the British consul Woodbine Parish. It established freedom of trade and navigation between the two countries, most-favored-nation treatment, freedom of worship and of residence for British subjects, and exemption from military service for them.

fuentes/tratado-con-gran-bretana-1825/po.texto: With it Great Britain recognized the independence of the United Provinces, and it provided the legal framework for British trade in the Río de la Plata throughout the 19th century.

fuentes/tratado-con-gran-bretana-1825/le.texto: Text in the Registro Nacional de las Provincias del Río de la Plata, on Wikisource

fuentes/ley-de-capitalizacion-1826/titul.texto: Law of capitalization of the city of Buenos Aires

fuentes/ley-de-capitalizacion-1826/autor.texto: General Constituent Congress of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata

fuentes/ley-de-capitalizacion-1826/resum.texto: Law passed on March 4, 1826 on the proposal of President Rivadavia. It declared the city of Buenos Aires and its surroundings the capital of the State, under the direct authority of the national government, and separated the rest of the province from it, whose institutions were dissolved.

fuentes/ley-de-capitalizacion-1826/por_q.texto: It left the nation with the city, the port and the customs house, and it provoked opposition from Buenos Aires Federalists. It lapsed when the national government dissolved in 1827, and the question of the capital remained open until 1880.

fuentes/ley-de-enfiteusis-1826/autor.texto: General Constituent Congress of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata

fuentes/ley-de-enfiteusis-1826/resumen.texto: Law of May 18, 1826 that extended nationwide the regime Buenos Aires had applied since 1822. Public lands, which guaranteed the debt, could not be sold; they were leased on long terms (enfiteusis) in exchange for a canon. The canon depended on valuations made by juries of residents of each zone, and the law did not limit the extension that each leaseholder could receive.

fuentes/ley-de-enfiteusis-1826/por_que_i.texto: It was the main instrument of the occupation of public land in Buenos Aires province in the 1820s and 1830s. Andrés Lamas defended it in the 19th century as progressive agrarian legislation, and Emilio Coni (1927) argued that it facilitated the formation of large latifundios.

fuentes/constitucion-de-1826/autor.texto: General Constituent Congress of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata

fuentes/constitucion-de-1826/resumen.texto: Constitution passed on December 24, 1826 that organized the country as a representative republic consolidated in a unified system. The president appointed the provincial governors from shortlists proposed by provincial administrative councils, and Congress had two chambers. It largely followed the text of the Constitution of 1819.

fuentes/constitucion-de-1826/por_que_imp.texto: It was rejected by almost all the provinces, which invoked the Fundamental Law of 1825, and its failure dissolved the national government in 1827. Some of its articles passed into the Constitution of 1853.

fuentes/leyes-de-la-florida-1825/titulo.texto: Declaration of Independence and Law of Union of the Eastern Province

fuentes/leyes-de-la-florida-1825/autor.texto: Chamber of Representatives of the Eastern Province

fuentes/leyes-de-la-florida-1825/resumen.texto: Three laws voted on August 25, 1825 in Florida by the Chamber of Representatives, meeting after the expedition of the Treinta y Tres Orientales. The first declared null the acts of incorporation into Portugal and Brazil and declared the province free of all foreign power. The second declared it united to the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, and the third set its flag.

fuentes/leyes-de-la-florida-1825/por_que.texto: The Law of Union was the basis of the request for incorporation that the Buenos Aires Congress accepted in October 1825, which led to war with Brazil. In Uruguay, August 25 is celebrated as independence day, and its meaning has been debated since the 19th century.

fuentes/leyes-de-la-florida-1825/leer.0..texto: Text of the three laws of August 25, 1825 on Wikisource

fuentes/convencion-garcia-1827/titulo.texto: Preliminary Peace Convention between the United Provinces and the Empire of Brazil (García Convention)

fuentes/convencion-garcia-1827/resumen.texto: Convention signed in Rio de Janeiro on May 24, 1827 by the envoy Manuel José García. In its first article the Republic renounced all rights over the Province of Montevideo, called Cisplatina, and recognized the integrity of the Empire. It further bound itself to withdraw its troops from the Banda Oriental, to return Martín García Island to its pre-war status and to pay the prizes that were shown to have been seized by its privateers through acts of piracy.

fuentes/convencion-garcia-1827/por_que_i.texto: It contradicted García’s instructions and the military victories of 1827. President Rivadavia and Congress rejected it, and the crisis led to Rivadavia’s resignation.

fuentes/convencion-garcia-1827/leer.0.ti.texto: Text on Wikisource, taken from the British and Foreign State Papers

fuentes/convencion-preliminar-de-paz-182.texto: Governments of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata and the Empire of Brazil

Treaty signed in Rio de Janeiro on August 27, 1828 with British mediation by Lord Ponsonby. The United Provinces and Brazil declared the Province of Montevideo independent. It was to give itself a constitution, which both governments would review before it was sworn, and they committed to help its legal government if a civil war threatened it within the following five years. An additional article guaranteed both countries free navigation of the Río de la Plata and its tributaries for fifteen years. The definitive treaty envisioned was never signed.
It ended the war with Brazil and created the Eastern State of Uruguay. The Eastern Missions, occupied by Rivera in 1828, were left to Brazil.
Text on Wikisource, from Antonio Díaz’s Historia política y militar de las Repúblicas del Plata (Political and Military History of the Republics of the Plate)

fuentes/constitucion-del-uruguay-1830/ti.texto: Constitution of the Oriental Republic of Uruguay of 1830

fuentes/constitucion-del-uruguay-1830/au.texto: General Constituent and Legislative Assembly of the Eastern State

fuentes/constitucion-del-uruguay-1830/re.texto: Constitution passed in 1829 and sworn on July 18, 1830, after being reviewed by Argentine and Brazilian commissioners, as the Convention of 1828 provided. It organized a unitary republic with a president elected by the General Assembly, a two-chamber Congress and Catholicism as the state religion. It suspended citizenship for paid servants, day laborers (peones jornaleros) and line soldiers.

fuentes/constitucion-del-uruguay-1830/po.texto: It gave legal form to the new State of Uruguay and remained in force until 1918.

fuentes/carta-de-varela-a-lavalle/titulo.texto: Letter from Juan Cruz Varela to Juan Lavalle (December 1828)

fuentes/carta-de-varela-a-lavalle/resume.texto: Letter that Juan Cruz Varela wrote to Lavalle from Buenos Aires after Dorrego’s defeat at Navarro (December 9, 1828) and before the execution. It argued that, after the blood shed at Navarro, “the process” for which he had made it flow was already formed. It ended: “Letters like this one are destroyed.” Lavalle kept it.

fuentes/carta-de-varela-a-lavalle/por_qu.texto: It is one of the documentary proofs that civilian Unitarian leaders urged Lavalle to execute Dorrego without trial. It became known when Ángel Justiniano Carranza published it around 1880.

fuentes/carta-de-varela-a-lavalle/leer.0.texto: Published in El general Lavalle ante la justicia póstuma (General Lavalle Before Posthumous Justice), by Ángel Justiniano Carranza (Internet Archive)

fuentes/cartas-del-carril-a-lavalle/titu.texto: Letters from Salvador María del Carril to Juan Lavalle (December 1828)

fuentes/cartas-del-carril-a-lavalle/resu.texto: Letters that Del Carril wrote to Lavalle in December 1828. In the one of the 12th, with Dorrego already imprisoned, he argued that “a revolution is a game of chance in which even the lives of the defeated are won when it is deemed necessary to dispose of them,” and urged him to settle the matter “in cold blood.” In another, written after the execution, he advised him to record the minutes of a verbal council that had never been held, adding that “if it is necessary to lie to posterity, one lies and deceives the living and the dead, as Machiavelli says.”

fuentes/cartas-del-carril-a-lavalle/por_.texto: They are the most cited document on civilian responsibility for Dorrego’s execution. Their publication in the 1880s damaged Del Carril’s reputation; he had been vice president of the Confederation.

fuentes/cartas-del-carril-a-lavalle/leer.texto: Published in El general Lavalle ante la justicia póstuma (General Lavalle Before Posthumous Justice), by Ángel Justiniano Carranza (Internet Archive)

fuentes/parte-de-lavalle-1828/titulo.texto: Lavalle’s report on the execution of Dorrego

fuentes/parte-de-lavalle-1828/resumen.texto: Note that Lavalle sent from Navarro on December 13, 1828 to the minister of the delegated government: “I inform the Delegated Government that Colonel Don Manuel Dorrego has just been executed by my order.” He added that “History” would judge impartially whether Dorrego had had to die or not, and that he had sacrificed him “to the tranquility of a people in mourning because of him.”

fuentes/parte-de-lavalle-1828/por_que_im.texto: It is the official record of the execution, which was carried out without trial or court-martial. With it Lavalle assumed sole responsibility, although civilian Unitarian leaders had urged him to do so.

fuentes/parte-de-lavalle-1828/leer.0.tit.texto: Published in El general Lavalle ante la justicia póstuma (General Lavalle Before Posthumous Justice), by Ángel Justiniano Carranza (Internet Archive)

fuentes/pacto-de-canuelas-1829/soporte.texto: Convention signed by Juan Lavalle and Juan Manuel de Rosas

fuentes/pacto-de-canuelas-1829/resumen.texto: Convention signed on June 24, 1829 at the Miller estancia, in Cañuelas, by Lavalle and Rosas. It ended hostilities in Buenos Aires province and provided for elections from a list agreed between the two parties, as well as an agreement on the provisional government. In a secret article both committed to present a unity list.

fuentes/pacto-de-canuelas-1829/por_que_i.texto: It was the first step of Lavalle’s negotiated exit. When the common list failed, the Pact of Barracas (August 1829) brought Viamonte to government and opened the way for Rosas.

fuentes/polemica-ferre-roxas/titulo.texto: Dispute between Pedro Ferré and José María Roxas y Patrón over trade and customs

fuentes/polemica-ferre-roxas/soporte.texto: Cross notes in the negotiations of the Federal Pact

fuentes/polemica-ferre-roxas/resumen.texto: Notes exchanged in 1830 in Santa Fe between the representative of Corrientes, Pedro Ferré, and the representative of Buenos Aires, José María Roxas y Patrón. Ferré asked for a congress to organize the country, for the customs revenues of Buenos Aires to be shared among all the provinces, for free navigation of the Paraná and Uruguay rivers, and for a ban or surcharge on imports that competed with the country’s products (textiles, wines, spirits). Roxas y Patrón replied that protection would make consumption more expensive and reduce trade and revenues, that local industry could not supply the country, and that it was not the moment for a congress.

fuentes/polemica-ferre-roxas/por_que_imp.texto: It is the classic text of the conflict between the port of Buenos Aires and the provinces over customs and rivers. The provinces argued that they paid taxes to the Buenos Aires customs house on what they consumed without receiving anything from that revenue. Corrientes did not sign the Federal Pact in January 1831 because of these differences.

fuentes/pacto-federal-1831/autor.texto: Governments of Buenos Aires, Santa Fe and Entre Ríos

fuentes/pacto-federal-1831/resumen.texto: Treaty signed in Santa Fe on January 4, 1831 by Buenos Aires, Santa Fe and Entre Ríos, which Corrientes joined in August. It was an offensive and defensive alliance against the League of the Interior, and it created a Representative Commission of the Litoral governments. Its article 16 charged that commission with inviting the other provinces, “when they are in full liberty and tranquility,” to a General Federative Congress to arrange the administration of the country, its internal and external trade, its navigation, the collection and distribution of general revenues and the payment of the debt.

fuentes/pacto-federal-1831/por_que_impor.texto: It was the legal bond of the Confederation during Rosas’s government, which never convened the congress. The Agreement of San Nicolás and the Constitution of 1853 invoke it as a preexisting pact.

fuentes/memorias-postumas-de-paz/titulo.texto: Posthumous Memoirs of General José María Paz

fuentes/memorias-postumas-de-paz/soporte.texto: Book published after the author’s death

fuentes/memorias-postumas-de-paz/resumen.texto: Memoirs that Paz wrote largely during his imprisonment (1831-1839) and that were published in 1855, a year after his death. They recount his campaigns in the independence and in the civil wars, the war with Brazil, La Tablada, Oncativo and his capture, with judgments on Quiroga, Lavalle and the caudillos from the point of view of a Unitarian soldier.

fuentes/memorias-postumas-de-paz/por_que.texto: They are one of the main sources for the civil wars. Lamadrid and other contemporaries published observations that disputed his version.

fuentes/memorias-postumas-de-paz/leer.0..texto: First volume of the 1855 edition (Internet Archive)

fuentes/observaciones-de-lamadrid/titulo.texto: Observations on the Posthumous Memoirs of Brigadier General Don José M. Paz

fuentes/observaciones-de-lamadrid/resume.texto: Response by Gregorio Aráoz de Lamadrid, published in 1855, to the judgments that Paz made about him in his memoirs. It discusses his conduct in the northern campaigns, in the war against Quiroga and in the League of the Interior.

fuentes/observaciones-de-lamadrid/por_qu.texto: It shows how the Unitarian chiefs themselves argued among themselves about the history of the civil wars.

fuentes/rough-notes-head/titulo.texto: Rough Notes Taken During Some Rapid Journeys Across the Pampas and Among the Andes

fuentes/rough-notes-head/resumen.texto: Account of Francis Bond Head’s journeys between Buenos Aires, Mendoza and Chile in 1825 and 1826, as the representative of a London mining company. It describes the post stations, the life of the gauchos, the distances and dangers of the pampas, and concludes that the mining business was not viable.

fuentes/rough-notes-head/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the most widely read British testimonies on Argentina in the Rivadavia era and on mining speculation in London in 1824-1825.

fuentes/protocolo-de-palermo/resumen.texto: Agreement signed on April 6, 1852 at Palermo de San Benito, Rosas’s former residence, by Urquiza and representatives of Buenos Aires, Corrientes and Santa Fe. It entrusted Urquiza with the foreign relations of the Confederation until a congress met, and it called the governors of all the provinces to a meeting to organize the country.

fuentes/protocolo-de-palermo/por_que_imp.texto: It was the first step of national organization after Caseros and led to the meeting of governors at San Nicolás.

fuentes/acuerdo-de-san-nicolas/autor.texto: Governors of the provinces of the Argentine Confederation

fuentes/acuerdo-de-san-nicolas/resumen.texto: Agreement signed on May 31, 1852 in San Nicolás de los Arroyos by the governors gathered by Urquiza, which the absent provinces later joined. It declared the Pact of 1831 in force, called a constituent congress in Santa Fe with two deputies per province regardless of population, and named Urquiza provisional director of the Confederation, with command of the military forces. Its article 19 provided that the provinces would contribute to national expenses with the proceeds of their external customs.

fuentes/acuerdo-de-san-nicolas/por_que_i.texto: Equal representation and article 19, which placed the revenue of the Buenos Aires customs house in the hands of the nation, led the Buenos Aires Legislature to reject the agreement in June 1852 and opened the separation of that province.

fuentes/constitucion-de-1853/resumen.texto: Constitution passed in Santa Fe on May 1, 1853, promulgated by Urquiza on May 25 and sworn on July 9, without Buenos Aires. It organized a federal representative republic with a president elected for six years without immediate re-election, a two-chamber Congress and a Supreme Court. It declared the external customs houses national and abolished the internal ones, opened river navigation to all flags, abolished slavery, guaranteed freedom of worship and mandated the promotion of European immigration. It fixed the capital in the city of Buenos Aires and allowed Congress to review the provincial constitutions.

fuentes/constitucion-de-1853/por_que_imp.texto: It is the basis of the current constitution, reformed in 1860, 1866, 1898, 1957 and 1994. The commission that drafted the project (Manuel Leiva, Juan María Gutiérrez, José Benjamín Gorostiaga, Pedro Díaz Colodrero and Pedro Ferré) took as its main models the Constitution of the United States and Alberdi’s Bases project, and also articles from the Argentine constitutions of 1819 and 1826. The liberal tradition saw it as the founding of the nation, and revisionist authors criticized it as an imported model that favored foreign trade.

fuentes/cartas-quillotanas/soporte.texto: Four letters published in 1853 under the title Cartas sobre la prensa y la política militante de la República Argentina (Letters on the Press and Militant Politics of the Argentine Republic)

fuentes/cartas-quillotanas/resumen.texto: Four letters that Alberdi wrote in Quillota (Chile) at the start of 1853, addressed to Sarmiento. He criticized the combat press Sarmiento was waging against Urquiza after Caseros, argued that armed or journalistic opposition to the government that was organizing the country prolonged the civil war, and defended support for the Confederation while the Constitution was being drafted.

fuentes/cartas-quillotanas/por_que_impor.texto: They opened the best-known controversy between the two main liberal writers of the period, who divided between Urquiza’s Confederation and Buenos Aires.

fuentes/las-ciento-y-una/resumen.texto: Sarmiento’s reply to the Quillota Letters, published in Santiago de Chile in 1853 in the form of letters. It defended his break with Urquiza, whom he accused of continuing Rosas’s system, and attacked Alberdi harshly and personally.

fuentes/las-ciento-y-una/por_que_importa.texto: It is the other side of the 1853 controversy and shows the division among the former anti-Rosas exiles after Caseros.

fuentes/las-ciento-y-una/leer.0.titulo.texto: Volume XV of Sarmiento’s Obras, 1897 (Internet Archive)

fuentes/comentarios-de-la-constitucion-s.texto: Commentaries on the Constitution of the Argentine Confederation

Book published by Sarmiento in Santiago de Chile in 1853, a few months after the Constitution was enacted. It comments on its articles, comparing them with the Constitution of the United States and with American case law and commentators, and argues that it should be interpreted along that model.

It was the first commentary on the Constitution of 1853 and the origin of the reading that understands it as an adaptation of the American model, as opposed to Alberdi’s, which stressed the differences.
Volume VIII of Sarmiento’s Obras, 1895 (Internet Archive)

fuentes/elementos-de-derecho-publico-pro.texto: Elements of Provincial Public Law for the Argentine Republic

Work that Alberdi published in Valparaíso in 1853 as a complement to the Bases, with principles and a model for the constitutions of the provinces within the federal system of the new Constitution. It argued that the provinces should organize their governments without contradicting the national Constitution, and that customs revenue was national.
It served as a guide to the provincial constitutions enacted after 1853. The Mendoza constitution (1854) followed the project Alberdi prepared for that province.

fuentes/campana-en-el-ejercito-grande/ti.texto: Campaign of the Grand Allied Army of South America

fuentes/campana-en-el-ejercito-grande/re.texto: Account by Sarmiento, who was a bulletin writer (boletinero) of Urquiza’s army, of the campaign that ended at Caseros and of the months that followed. It includes his conflict with Urquiza, whom he accuses of keeping the forms of Rosismo, such as the punzó emblem.

fuentes/campana-en-el-ejercito-grande/po.texto: It is a direct testimony of Caseros and of the beginning of the rupture between Urquiza and the liberals who had accompanied him.

fuentes/campana-en-el-ejercito-grande/le.texto: Works of Sarmiento, vol. XIV (1897), on Internet Archive

fuentes/sermon-de-esquiu-1853/titulo.texto: Sermon of Mamerto Esquiú at the Swearing-In of the Constitution

fuentes/sermon-de-esquiu-1853/escrita.lu.texto: San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca

fuentes/sermon-de-esquiu-1853/resumen.texto: Sermon preached by the Franciscan friar Mamerto Esquiú in the main church of Catamarca on July 9, 1853, the day the Constitution was sworn in that province. It presented the Constitution as the end of forty years of civil wars and called for submission to it as to a sacred law, even though it was imperfect.

fuentes/sermon-de-esquiu-1853/por_que_im.texto: It was printed and circulated throughout the country, and it was the best-known clerical voice in favor of the Constitution.

fuentes/tratados-de-libre-navegacion-185.texto: Treaties of Free Navigation of the Paraná and Uruguay Rivers
Argentine Confederation, Great Britain, France and the United States
Three treaties with the same content, signed by Salvador María del Carril and José Benjamín Gorostiaga with the representatives of each country

Treaties signed on July 10, 1853, in San José de Flores, in Urquiza’s camp during the siege of Buenos Aires, with Great Britain, France and the United States. The Confederation declared free navigation of the Paraná and Uruguay rivers for merchant ships of all nations, and the powers committed to respect that freedom even in case of war; Martín García Island was not to remain in the hands of a state that did not accept that principle.

They settled, for the Confederation, the river question that had led to the blockades of the 1840s, and allowed the Litoral ports and Paraguay to trade directly with the outside world without passing through Buenos Aires, which did not recognize them.
Treaty with Great Britain, on Wikisource
Treaty with the United States, on Wikisource

fuentes/estatuto-de-hacienda-fragueiro/t.texto: Statute for the Organization of the Treasury and Public Credit

fuentes/estatuto-de-hacienda-fragueiro/r.texto: Statute decreed at the end of 1853 on the initiative of Minister Mariano Fragueiro, which created a national bank with the monopoly on currency issue, in charge of collecting revenues and managing public credit. The bills declared legal tender were rejected by the provinces, and the bank closed in 1854.

fuentes/estatuto-de-hacienda-fragueiro/p.texto: It was the Confederation’s first attempt to have its own treasury without the Buenos Aires customs house; its failure showed the lack of resources of the Paraná government.

fuentes/constitucion-del-estado-de-bueno.texto: Constitution of the State of Buenos Aires
General Legislative Assembly of the State of Buenos Aires

Constitution enacted in April 1854 by the Porteño Legislature after the siege of Lagos. It declared Buenos Aires “a State with the free exercise of its internal and external sovereignty, as long as it does not expressly delegate it to a federal Government,” organized a governor, a two-chamber legislature and municipalities, and fixed boundaries that included lands to the south as far as Patagonia.
It gave legal form to the separation of Buenos Aires from the Confederation, which lasted until 1860; it left the customs house and the revenue of its port in the hands of the Porteño State.

fuentes/ley-de-derechos-diferenciales/re.texto: Law of the Confederation’s Congress, enacted in 1856, which charged double the ordinary duty on foreign goods that entered the Confederation’s ports after having been landed at another port on the Río de la Plata, that is, in Buenos Aires or Montevideo. A later law applied the same criterion to exports.

fuentes/ley-de-derechos-diferenciales/po.texto: It aimed to have foreign trade reach Rosario and the Confederation’s other ports directly, without passing through the Buenos Aires customs house; Buenos Aires took it as an aggression, and its results were smaller than expected.

fuentes/censo-de-buenos-aires-1855/titul.texto: Census of the City of Buenos Aires of 1855

fuentes/censo-de-buenos-aires-1855/autor.texto: Government of the State of Buenos Aires

fuentes/censo-de-buenos-aires-1855/resum.texto: Census of the city of Buenos Aires taken in 1855, during the separation of the State of Buenos Aires. The most cited figure is 90,076 inhabitants, almost double the some 45,000 estimated for the end of the viceroyalty, with an already significant presence of European immigrants.

fuentes/censo-de-buenos-aires-1855/por_q.texto: It is one of the bases for measuring the city’s growth between the population registers of the first half of the century and the national census of 1869.

fuentes/descripcion-de-moussy/titulo.texto: Geographical and Statistical Description of the Argentine Confederation

fuentes/descripcion-de-moussy/resumen.texto: Work in three volumes and an atlas that Martin de Moussy published in Paris between 1860 and 1864, with support from the Confederation’s government. It describes the geography, climate, population, production and communication routes of each province, with data gathered during his travels between 1855 and 1859.

fuentes/descripcion-de-moussy/por_que_im.texto: It was the most complete description of the country before the 1869 census, and it sought to attract European immigrants and capital.

fuentes/pacto-de-san-jose-de-flores/titu.texto: Pact of San José de Flores

fuentes/pacto-de-san-jose-de-flores/auto.texto: Argentine Confederation and State of Buenos Aires

fuentes/pacto-de-san-jose-de-flores/sopo.texto: Signed with the mediation of Francisco Solano López, envoy of Paraguay

fuentes/pacto-de-san-jose-de-flores/resu.texto: Peace and union agreement signed on November 11, 1859, after Cepeda, with the mediation of the Paraguayan Francisco Solano López. Buenos Aires declared itself an integral part of the Confederation and could propose reforms to the Constitution through a provincial convention. Customs passed to the nation, but this guaranteed Buenos Aires for five years its 1859 budget, and Porteño customs laws would remain in force until Congress unified the tariffs.

fuentes/pacto-de-san-jose-de-flores/por_.texto: It set the conditions for Buenos Aires’s reincorporation and led to the constitutional reform of 1860.

fuentes/convenio-de-union-1860/autor.texto: Argentine Confederation and State of Buenos Aires

fuentes/convenio-de-union-1860/resumen.texto: Agreement signed in June 1860 between President Derqui and the government of Buenos Aires to complete the Pact of San José de Flores. It provided for the convening of a national convention to examine the reforms proposed by the Porteño convention and the terms of Buenos Aires’s incorporation.

fuentes/convenio-de-union-1860/por_que_i.texto: It opened the way to the Santa Fe Convention of September 1860.

fuentes/reforma-constitucional-1860/resu.texto: Amendments to the Constitution of 1853 approved in September 1860 by a national convention meeting in Santa Fe, at the proposal of the Buenos Aires convention. The capital ceased to be fixed in the city of Buenos Aires and came to depend on a law of Congress; Congress lost the power to review provincial constitutions; Congress was prohibited from restricting freedom of the press; and the article on unenumerated rights was added. The country was allowed to be also called the Argentine Republic and the Argentine Nation.

fuentes/reforma-constitucional-1860/por_.texto: With it Buenos Aires accepted the Constitution; the reform strengthened the autonomy of the provinces, and in particular that of Buenos Aires.

fuentes/reforma-constitucional-1860/leer.texto: Text of the Constitution with the 1860 reforms, on Wikisource

fuentes/carta-de-mayo-1825/soporte.texto: First constitution of the province of San Juan

fuentes/carta-de-mayo-1825/resumen.texto: First constitution of the province of San Juan, enacted in 1825 at the impulse of Governor Salvador María del Carril. It declared the rights of the inhabitants and admitted the practice of other religions besides Catholicism, which in July of that year provoked a rebellion that overthrew Del Carril.

fuentes/carta-de-mayo-1825/por_que_impor.texto: It shows the scope and limits of the liberal reforms of the 1820s in the interior: religious freedom was the central motive of the reaction.

fuentes/travels-in-chile-and-la-plata/ti.texto: Travels in Chile and La Plata

fuentes/travels-in-chile-and-la-plata/re.texto: Two-volume book by the British engineer John Miers, published in London in 1826, about his travels and residence in Chile and his time in Buenos Aires and the pampas between 1818 and 1825. It describes the geography, economy, government and customs, and the difficulties of British industrial ventures.

fuentes/travels-in-chile-and-la-plata/po.texto: It is one of the traveler accounts that shaped the British image of the Río de la Plata in the years of recognition and of the first loans.

fuentes/travels-in-chile-and-la-plata/le.texto: First volume of the London edition of 1826 (Internet Archive)

fuentes/letters-on-paraguay/soporte.texto: Written with his brother William Parish Robertson

fuentes/letters-on-paraguay/resumen.texto: Letters published in London in 1838 by the brothers John and William Parish Robertson about the years John lived in Asunción as a merchant, during the rise of José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia. They describe Paraguay’s trade, its society and Francia’s government, which ended by expelling the authors.

fuentes/letters-on-paraguay/por_que_impo.texto: It is one of the few direct accounts of Paraguay in Francia’s early years, written from a perspective hostile to his government.

fuentes/letters-on-paraguay/leer.0.titul.texto: Second volume of the London edition of 1838 (Internet Archive)

fuentes/estudios-sobre-la-constitucion-a.texto: Studies on the Argentine Constitution of 1853

Alberdi’s reply to Sarmiento’s Commentaries, published in Valparaíso in 1853. It held that the Constitution of 1853 was not a copy of that of the United States but an adaptation to Argentine conditions, largely taken from his own project, and that it should be interpreted in light of those conditions.
It opened a debate that continued in Argentine constitutional law about how far the Constitution should be read in light of the model and case law of the United States.

fuentes/cuestiones-argentinas-fragueiro/.texto: Book that Mariano Fragueiro wrote in Chile and published in 1852, on the public finances, currency and credit of the future Argentine organization. It proposed that credit and the issue of currency be functions of the State through a national bank, an idea he applied as Minister of Finance of the Confederation.
It is one of the few Argentine economic proposals of the period that did not follow Alberdi’s liberalism and placed credit in the hands of the State.

fuentes/tratado-de-1856-con-chile/titulo.texto: Treaty of Peace, Friendship, Commerce and Navigation between Chile and the Argentine Confederation

fuentes/tratado-de-1856-con-chile/autor.texto: Governments of Chile and the Argentine Confederation

fuentes/tratado-de-1856-con-chile/resume.texto: Treaty signed in Santiago on August 30, 1855 and ratified in 1856. It established that the boundaries between the two countries would be those they had as Spanish possessions in 1810, postponed the question of Patagonia, Tierra del Fuego and the Strait of Magellan, and provided for resolving differences by direct negotiation or arbitration.

fuentes/tratado-de-1856-con-chile/por_qu.texto: It was the first boundary treaty between Argentina and Chile and the starting point of the southern dispute that was resolved by the 1881 treaty.

personas/francisco-ramirez/resumen.texto: Caudillo from Entre Ríos, lieutenant of Artigas, who together with Estanislao López defeated the Directory at Cepeda (1820) and signed the Treaty of Pilar. He broke with Artigas, defeated him, and created the Republic of Entre Ríos (1820–1821); he died in 1821 in a campaign against Santa Fe and Buenos Aires, and López had his head displayed in the Cabildo of Santa Fe.

personas/estanislao-lopez/resumen.texto: Governor of Santa Fe from 1818 until his death. Victor at Cepeda (1820) together with Ramírez, he signed the Treaty of Benegas with Buenos Aires and the Federal Pact of 1831, and his army captured General Paz in 1831. He was Rosas’s main ally in the Litoral.

personas/juan-bautista-bustos/resumen.texto: Army of the North officer who led the Arequito mutiny (1820), which left the Directory without its army. He governed Córdoba from 1820 to 1829, opposed the Constitution of 1826 and was defeated by José María Paz at San Roque (1829).

personas/facundo-quiroga/resumen.texto: Caudillo from La Rioja who dominated the interior between 1826 and 1835. He defeated Lamadrid at El Tala (1826) and Rincón de Valladares (1827), was defeated by Paz at La Tablada (1829) and Oncativo (1830), and destroyed the League of the Interior at La Ciudadela (1831). He was assassinated at Barranca Yaco in 1835; Sarmiento made him the central figure of Facundo: Civilization and Barbarism (1845).

personas/juan-felipe-ibarra/resumen.texto: Military man from Santiago del Estero who in 1820 separated Santiago del Estero from the province of Tucumán and governed it, with brief interruptions, until his death in 1851. He adhered to the Federal Pact and was an ally of Quiroga and Rosas.

personas/gregorio-araoz-de-lamadrid/resu.texto: Military man from Tucumán in the wars of independence and Unitarian leader in the civil wars. He governed Tucumán from 1825 and was defeated by Quiroga at El Tala (1826), Rincón de Valladares (1827) and La Ciudadela (1831); he left memoirs of his military life.

personas/martin-rodriguez/resumen.texto: Governor of Buenos Aires from 1820 to 1824. His government, with Rivadavia and Manuel José García as ministers, abolished the cabildos, enacted the electoral law of 1821, founded the University of Buenos Aires, and reformed the Church and the administration.

personas/rivadavia/resumen.texto: Minister of Government of Buenos Aires between 1821 and 1824 and first president of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata (1826–1827). He promoted the ecclesiastical reform, the university, the Banco de Descuentos, the Baring loan, emphyteusis and the unitary Constitution of 1826; he resigned in 1827 after the rejection of the García Convention and died in exile in Cádiz. Liberal historiography presented him as the founder of the institutions; revisionist historiography, as responsible for the indebtedness and Porteño centralism.

personas/manuel-jose-garcia/resumen.texto: Minister of Finance of Buenos Aires in the 1820s and negotiator of the 1825 treaty with Great Britain. Sent to Rio de Janeiro in 1827, he signed the convention recognizing the Banda Oriental as part of the Empire of Brazil, which the government and Congress rejected. He later served as minister under Rosas and Viamonte.

personas/julian-segundo-de-aguero/resume.texto: Porteño priest and one of the leaders of the Unitarian party in the 1820s. Deputy in the Junta de Representantes and in the Congress of 1824–1827, he defended the ecclesiastical reform and the Constitution of 1826, and was Rivadavia’s minister during his presidency.

personas/woodbine-parish/resumen.texto: First British consul general in Buenos Aires, who signed in 1825 the treaty of friendship, commerce and navigation that recognized the United Provinces. In 1839 he published in London a description of Buenos Aires and the provinces of the Río de la Plata based on documents he gathered in the country.

personas/george-canning/resumen.texto: British Secretary of Foreign Affairs between 1822 and 1827. His government recognized in 1824–1825 the independence of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, Mexico and Gran Colombia through treaties of friendship and commerce that gave guarantees to British merchants.

personas/juan-antonio-lavalleja/resumen.texto: Artigas’s officer who in 1825 led the expedition of the Treinta y Tres Orientales against Brazilian rule. He was governor of the Eastern Province during the war with Brazil and a rival of Rivera in the politics of the new State.

personas/fructuoso-rivera/resumen.texto: Eastern caudillo who served Artigas, the Portuguese and the Brazilians, and joined the insurrection in 1825. In 1828 he occupied the Eastern Missions; he was the first constitutional president of Uruguay (1830–1834) and leader of the Colorado party.

personas/manuel-oribe/resumen.texto: One of the Treinta y Tres Orientales and second constitutional president of Uruguay (1835–1838). Overthrown by Rivera, he led the Blanco party and, as an ally of Rosas, besieged Montevideo during the Guerra Grande (1843–1851).

personas/carlos-federico-lecor/resumen.texto: Portuguese general who occupied Montevideo in 1817 and governed the Banda Oriental, which was incorporated in 1821 into the kingdom of Portugal as the Cisplatine Province and from 1822 into the Empire of Brazil. He led the Brazilian forces at the start of the war of 1825–1828.

personas/pedro-i-de-brasil/resumen.texto: Son of John VI of Portugal, he proclaimed the independence of Brazil in 1822 and was its first emperor. He declared war on the United Provinces in December 1825 over the Banda Oriental, signed the peace of 1828 and abdicated in 1831 in favor of his son Pedro II.

personas/pedro-ii-de-brasil/resumen.texto: Emperor of Brazil from 1831, with a regency until 1840, until the proclamation of the republic in 1889. His government allied with Urquiza and Montevideo against Rosas in 1851 and with Mitre and Flores in the war against Paraguay.

personas/marques-de-barbacena/nombre.texto: Felisberto Caldeira Brant, Marquis of Barbacena

personas/marques-de-barbacena/resumen.texto: Brazilian military man and politician who commanded the imperial army at the battle of Ituzaingó (1827), where he was defeated by the republican army of Carlos María de Alvear.

personas/john-ponsonby/resumen.texto: British diplomat sent to Buenos Aires in 1826 and then to Rio de Janeiro. His mediation led to the Preliminary Peace Convention of 1828, which created an independent Eastern State instead of handing the Banda Oriental to either of the two contenders; his correspondence shows British interest in a Río de la Plata open to trade.

personas/manuel-dorrego/resumen.texto: Military man of the independence and leader of the Porteño federal party, opponent of Rivadavia and of the Constitution of 1826. Governor of Buenos Aires from 1827, he signed the peace with Brazil in 1828; overthrown by the mutiny of December 1 of that year, he was executed without trial on Lavalle’s orders at Navarro on December 13.

personas/juan-lavalle/resumen.texto: Officer of San Martín’s campaigns and of the war with Brazil. He led the Unitarian mutiny of December 1, 1828 and ordered the execution of Dorrego; defeated at Puente de Márquez (1829), he signed with Rosas the pacts of Cañuelas and Barracas. He returned to war against Rosas in 1839 and died in Jujuy in 1841.

personas/salvador-maria-del-carril/resum.texto: Governor of San Juan (1823–1825), where his Carta de Mayo provoked a rebellion, and minister of Rivadavia. In December 1828 he wrote letters to Lavalle urging him to execute Dorrego. He was a constituent delegate in 1853, vice president of the Confederation with Urquiza (1854–1860) and a judge of the Supreme Court.

personas/juan-cruz-varela/resumen.texto: Neoclassical poet and Unitarian journalist, author of odes to Rivadavia’s reforms and of the tragedies Dido and Argia. In December 1828 he wrote Lavalle a letter urging him to execute Dorrego; he died in exile in Montevideo.

personas/jose-maria-paz/resumen.texto: General from Córdoba who defeated Bustos (1829) and Quiroga at La Tablada (1829) and Oncativo (1830), and led the League of the Interior. He was captured in 1831 by a Santa Fe party and spent almost eight years in prison; his posthumous Memoirs (1855) are a main source on the civil wars.

personas/pedro-ferre/resumen.texto: Governor of Corrientes in four terms between 1824 and 1842. In the negotiations of the Federal Pact (1830–1831) he demanded protection for the country’s production, free navigation of the rivers, the sharing of the Buenos Aires customs revenues and a congress to organize the country; because of these differences Corrientes only joined the pact in August 1831.

personas/jose-maria-roxas-y-patron/resum.texto: Porteño merchant, last president of the Congress of 1824–1827 and minister of finance under Dorrego and Rosas. He represented Buenos Aires before Ferré in 1830, defended free trade and the preservation of the Porteño customs house, signed the Federal Pact and was the Porteño delegate on the Representative Commission until he withdrew in 1832.

personas/manuel-leiva/resumen.texto: Santa Fe lawyer who in 1831 represented Corrientes on the Representative Commission of the Litoral provinces, where he demanded the convening of the congress provided for in the Federal Pact. An opponent of Rosas, he was a deputy in the constituent Congress of 1853.

personas/jose-vicente-reinafe/resumen.texto: Governor of Córdoba between 1831 and 1835, with the support of Estanislao López. He and his brothers were accused of organizing Quiroga’s murder at Barranca Yaco; tried in Buenos Aires, he was executed at the Plaza de la Victoria on October 25, 1837.

personas/urquiza/resumen.texto: Governor of Entre Ríos from 1841, an ally of Rosas until his pronouncement of 1851. He defeated Rosas at Caseros (1852), signed the Agreement of San Nicolás, promulgated the Constitution of 1853 and was the first constitutional president of the Confederation (1854–1860). He defeated Buenos Aires at Cepeda (1859) and withdrew from the field at Pavón (1861); he was assassinated at the Palacio San José in 1870.

personas/santiago-derqui/resumen.texto: Córdoba lawyer, Urquiza’s minister of the interior and president of the Confederation from 1860. His government failed to integrate Buenos Aires; after Pavón he resigned in November 1861 and went into exile in Montevideo.

personas/juan-esteban-pedernera/resumen.texto: Officer of San Martín’s army and vice president under Derqui. When Derqui resigned, he held the presidency and on December 12, 1861 declared the national government in recess, which left the Confederation dissolved.

personas/valentin-alsina/resumen.texto: Unitarian jurist, exiled during Rosas’s government. He was governor of Buenos Aires after the revolution of September 11, 1852 and between 1857 and 1859, and he upheld the separation of the State of Buenos Aires from the Confederation; he resigned after the defeat at Cepeda.

personas/hilario-lagos/resumen.texto: Porteño federal military man who in December 1852 revolted in the countryside against the Buenos Aires government that arose from the revolution of September 11 and besieged the city until July 1853, with Urquiza’s support.

personas/pastor-obligado/resumen.texto: First governor of the State of Buenos Aires under the Porteño constitution of 1854, between 1853 and 1857. During his government the Western Railway was built and the administration of the separate State was organized.

personas/jose-benjamin-gorostiaga/resume.texto: Lawyer from Santiago del Estero who, in the Congress of Santa Fe, drafted with Juan María Gutiérrez the project of the Constitution of 1853 and defended it as reporting member. He was Urquiza’s minister and president of the Supreme Court.

personas/juan-francisco-segui/resumen.texto: Lawyer and journalist from Santa Fe who accompanied Urquiza in the negotiations for the Agreement of San Nicolás and was a deputy for Santa Fe in the constituent Congress of 1853, where he opposed requiring the president to be Catholic. He later served as minister of foreign affairs of the Confederation.

personas/facundo-zuviria/resumen.texto: Jurist from Salta, president of the constituent Congress of Santa Fe. In April 1853 he asked that the enactment of the Constitution be postponed until there was peace and Buenos Aires took part, and he was left in the minority.

personas/mariano-fragueiro/resumen.texto: Merchant and financier from Córdoba, author of Argentine Questions (1852). As Minister of Finance of the Confederation (1853–1854) he decreed a statute creating a national bank with the monopoly on issue; paper money was not accepted and the system failed. He later became governor of Córdoba.

personas/mamerto-esquiu/activo.lugar.texto: San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca

personas/mamerto-esquiu/resumen.texto: Franciscan friar from Catamarca. On July 9, 1853 he preached in Catamarca a sermon calling for obedience to the new Constitution; he was bishop of Córdoba from 1880. The Catholic Church beatified him in 2021.

personas/nazario-benavidez/resumen.texto: Federal governor of San Juan between 1836 and 1855, with interruptions. Displaced by the liberals, he was murdered in prison in October 1858, an act that deepened the confrontation between the Confederation and Buenos Aires.

personas/antonino-aberastain/resumen.texto: Lawyer from San Juan, liberal governor of San Juan after the assassination of José Antonio Virasoro (1860). Defeated at Rinconada del Pocito by the federal forces of Juan Saá, he was executed by firing squad the next day, January 12, 1861.

personas/juan-saa/resumen.texto: Federal military man from San Luis, governor of San Luis. In January 1861 he was sent as federal intervenor to San Juan, defeated Aberastain at Rinconada del Pocito, and was charged with the execution of the prisoners.

personas/carlos-antonio-lopez/resumen.texto: Consul (1841–1844) and president of Paraguay (1844–1862). He formally declared independence in 1842, which the Argentine Confederation recognized in 1852, opened the country to trade and modernized the State; he was succeeded by his son Francisco Solano López.

personas/aaron-castellanos/resumen.texto: Businessman from Salta who in 1853 signed a contract with the government of Santa Fe to bring families of European farmers. With them the colony of Esperanza was founded in 1856, which is usually considered the first organized agricultural colony in the country.

personas/martin-de-moussy/resumen.texto: French physician and naturalist who toured the Confederation at Urquiza’s behest and published in Paris a geographical and statistical description of the country (1860–1864) with an atlas.

personas/francis-bond-head/resumen.texto: British military man sent in 1825 by a London mining company to explore mines in the United Provinces. His travel notes on the pampas and the Andes (1826) were widely read in Great Britain.

personas/antonio-saenz/resumen.texto: Porteño priest and jurist, deputy in the Congress of Tucumán. He was the first rector of the University of Buenos Aires, from its inauguration in 1821 until his death in 1825, and organized its first law studies.

personas/john-parish-robertson/resumen.texto: Scottish merchant who lived in Francia’s Paraguay and in Buenos Aires. With his brother William he took part in placing the Baring loan and organized the Scottish colony of Monte Grande (1825); together they published in London letters on Paraguay and South America.

personas/miguel-estanislao-soler/resumen.texto: Military officer from Buenos Aires who fought in the British invasions, was governor of the Banda Oriental in 1814 and served in the Army of the Andes. After the fall of the Directorate he became governor of Buenos Aires in June 1820: the Cabildo of Luján and the army named him on the 17th, and the legislature recognized him on the 23rd. Estanislao López defeated him on the 28th at Cañada de la Cruz, and he fled to Montevideo. In the war against Brazil, according to the Spanish-language article, he commanded the 3rd Corps at Ituzaingó. The two biographies differ on his withdrawal under Rosas. The Spanish-language one says that in 1830 Rosas appointed him commander of the urban forces and that in 1840, because of the repression, he went to Montevideo and returned the following year. The English-language one says that in 1829 he resigned his posts, settled in the Banda Oriental and returned to Buenos Aires in 1837.

personas/caesar-augustus-rodney/resumen.texto: Lawyer and politician from Delaware, U.S. Attorney General from 1807 to 1811, and senator. In 1817 he was on the commission sent by Monroe to South America and, with John Graham, published in 1819 a report defending recognition of the new republics. Appointed minister plenipotentiary to the United Provinces in January 1823, he presented his credentials on December 27, 1823, and with that diplomatic relations between the two countries were established, according to the article “Embajada de Argentina en Estados Unidos”. He died in Buenos Aires on June 10, 1824, and Forbes succeeded him as chargé d'affaires.

hechos/motin-de-arequito/resumen.texto: On January 8, 1820 the Army of the North, which the Directory had called to fight the caudillos of the Litoral, revolted at the post of Arequito (Santa Fe) under the command of Juan Bautista Bustos, José María Paz and Alejandro Heredia. It refused to continue the civil war and returned to Córdoba, leaving the Directory without its main army before Cepeda.

hechos/anarquia-del-ano-20/resumen.texto: After the defeat at Cepeda (February 1, 1820) the Directory and the Congress were dissolved, and each province began to govern itself. Buenos Aires had several governors in a few months, until in September Martín Rodríguez was elected, backed by the countryside militias of Juan Manuel de Rosas, who in October defeated a mutiny in the city.

hechos/republica-de-entre-rios/resumen.texto: Francisco Ramírez, after defeating Artigas, organized in September 1820 the Republic of Entre Ríos, which united Entre Ríos, Corrientes and Misiones under his command as supreme chief. It had its own regulations for administration, justice and militias, and it was dissolved in 1821 after Ramírez’s death.

hechos/firma-del-tratado-de-benegas/resu.texto: Buenos Aires and Santa Fe signed peace on November 24, 1820 at the Benegas estancia, with the mediation of Córdoba. Rosas guaranteed the delivery of 25,000 head of cattle to Santa Fe, and the peace left Ramírez alone against the two provinces.

hechos/muerte-de-francisco-ramirez/resum.texto: Defeated by the forces of Santa Fe and Buenos Aires and pursued to the north of Córdoba, Ramírez died on July 10, 1821 in a combat with a party that caught up with him. Estanislao López had his head displayed in Santa Fe, and with his death the Republic of Entre Ríos was dissolved.

hechos/firma-del-tratado-del-cuadrilater.texto: Buenos Aires, Santa Fe, Entre Ríos and Corrientes signed in Santa Fe, on January 25, 1822, a treaty of peace and alliance guaranteeing their territory and free trade among them. Following Buenos Aires, which had already withdrawn from the congress that Bustos had convened in Córdoba, the other three committed not to enter a congress for now, and the Córdoba congress dissolved.

hechos/gobierno-de-martin-rodriguez/titu.texto: Government of Martín Rodríguez in Buenos Aires

hechos/gobierno-de-martin-rodriguez/resu.texto: Martín Rodríguez governed the province of Buenos Aires from 1820 to 1824 with Bernardino Rivadavia and Manuel José García as ministers. With peace with Santa Fe and the customs revenue of the port, his government undertook the administrative, ecclesiastical, educational and financial reforms known as the Rivadavian reforms.

hechos/ley-electoral-de-1821/resumen.texto: The law of August 14, 1821 established that the deputies of the Junta de Representantes were to be elected by direct vote of all free men aged twenty or over, native or resident, while to be elected one had to own property. That same year the Junta abolished the province’s cabildos. The law greatly expanded the number of voters; studies such as those by Marcela Ternavasio show that elections ended up, in practice, in the hands of those who could mobilize those voters.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-universidad-de-bu.texto: Founding of the University of Buenos Aires

The government of Martín Rodríguez, on Rivadavia’s initiative, created the University of Buenos Aires, which was inaugurated on August 12, 1821 with the priest Antonio Sáenz as its first rector. It brought together in departments the elementary, preparatory, medical, exact sciences, jurisprudence and sacred sciences studies that existed in the city.

hechos/reforma-eclesiastica-de-rivadavia.texto: The clergy reform law of December 1822 abolished ecclesiastical jurisdiction (fuero) and tithes, which it replaced with a state budget for worship, and closed convents of male orders, whose property passed to the State. In March 1823 a group of opponents led by Gregorio Tagle attempted a revolution against the government, which failed.

hechos/fundacion-del-cementerio-de-la-re.texto: Opening of the Cementerio del Norte (Recoleta Cemetery)

The government of Buenos Aires opened in 1822 the city’s first public cemetery in the orchard of the convent of the Recoleta Franciscans, suppressed by the ecclesiastical reform. Until then the dead were buried in the churches and their atriums.

hechos/fundacion-del-banco-de-descuentos.texto: Creation of the Banco de Descuentos

A law of June 1822 created the Banco de Descuentos, of private capital and with the power to issue banknotes, which was run by the city’s large merchants. In 1826 it was absorbed by the National Bank, whose legal tender notes financed the war with Brazil and depreciated quickly; the current Banco de la Provincia de Buenos Aires descends from that institution.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-sociedad-de-benef.texto: Founding of the Sociedad de Beneficencia

A decree of January 2, 1823, promoted by Minister Rivadavia, created the Sociedad de Beneficencia, made up of women from leading Buenos Aires families, which was put in charge of the girls’ schools, the Casa de Niños Expósitos and the women’s hospitals. It was the first public institution run by women in the country and operated until its dissolution in 1948.

hechos/fundacion-del-colegio-de-ciencias.texto: Founding of the Colegio de Ciencias Morales

In 1823 Rivadavia reorganized the old Colegio de la Unión del Sud as the Colegio de Ciencias Morales, with scholarships for students from the provinces; among them studied Juan Bautista Alberdi and Marco Avellaneda. It is a direct antecedent of the Colegio Nacional de Buenos Aires, created in 1863.

hechos/emprestito-baring/resumen.texto: Authorized by a Porteño law of 1822 for works such as the port of Buenos Aires and new frontier towns, the loan of one million nominal pounds was placed in London in 1824 through the house of Baring Brothers. Buenos Aires received 70% of the nominal value, less commissions and interest paid in advance, and the planned works were not carried out; it stopped paying in 1827, resumed payments in 1857 and finished paying it off at the beginning of the 20th century. Revisionist authors, such as Scalabrini Ortiz, presented it as a British swindle, and later economic historiography points out that these conditions were usual in Latin American loans of the time, almost all of which ended in default.

hechos/congreso-general-de-1824/resumen.texto: The congress of deputies from all the provinces convened in Buenos Aires on December 16, 1824 and enacted the Fundamental Law (1825), accepted the incorporation of the Banda Oriental, created the presidency, made Buenos Aires the capital and enacted the Constitution of 1826. Once that constitution was rejected by the provinces, the congress dissolved in August 1827.

hechos/reconocimiento-britanico-1825/tit.texto: British Recognition of the United Provinces

hechos/reconocimiento-britanico-1825/res.texto: On February 2, 1825 Manuel José García and consul Woodbine Parish signed the treaty of friendship, commerce and navigation by which Great Britain recognized the independence of the United Provinces. The treaty guaranteed British subjects trade, residence and worship in the Río de la Plata.

hechos/colonia-escocesa-de-monte-grande/.texto: In 1825 some two hundred Scottish settlers hired by the Parish Robertson brothers arrived in Buenos Aires and settled on the Santa Catalina estancia, in Monte Grande. The colony, one of the first colonies of European farmers in the country, dispersed in the late 1820s due to wars and debts.

hechos/presidencia-de-rivadavia/resumen.texto: The Congress created the presidency on February 6, 1826, before there was a constitution, and the next day elected Rivadavia. His government made Buenos Aires the capital, created the Banco Nacional, extended emphyteusis and directed the war with Brazil, while the provinces rejected the Constitution of 1826 and Quiroga defeated the governments allied with the president. He resigned on June 27, 1827, after the rejection of the García Convention.

hechos/batalla-de-el-tala/lugar.texto: El Tala, on the border of Tucumán and Salta

hechos/batalla-de-el-tala/resumen.texto: Facundo Quiroga defeated on October 27, 1826 the governor of Tucumán, Gregorio Aráoz de Lamadrid, who supported the policy of the national government. It was the beginning of the war of the interior caudillos against Rivadavia’s presidency.

hechos/rechazo-de-la-constitucion-de-182.texto: Most provinces, among them Córdoba, Santa Fe, Entre Ríos, Santiago del Estero and La Rioja, rejected the unitary Constitution or refused to consider it, invoking the Fundamental Law of 1825. The governments of Bustos, Quiroga and Ibarra allied against Rivadavia’s government.

hechos/batalla-de-rincon-de-valladares/r.texto: Quiroga defeated Lamadrid again on July 6, 1827 in Tucumán and emerged as the most powerful military leader of the interior.

hechos/presidencia-de-vicente-lopez-y-pl.texto: Presidency of Vicente López y Planes

After Rivadavia’s resignation, Congress elected Vicente López y Planes provisional president in early July 1827. His function was to liquidate the national government: he restored the province of Buenos Aires, whose legislature elected Manuel Dorrego governor, and on August 18 Congress dissolved and López resigned.

hechos/cruzada-de-los-treinta-y-tres-ori.texto: Landing of the Treinta y Tres Orientales

On April 19, 1825 a group of Easterners led by Juan Antonio Lavalleja, who had left Buenos Aires with the support of Porteño estancieros, landed at the Playa de la Agraciada to rise up the Banda Oriental against the Empire of Brazil. Within a few weeks Fructuoso Rivera joined them and the Eastern countryside rose up.

hechos/congreso-de-la-florida/resumen.texto: The Chamber of Representatives of the Eastern Province, meeting in Florida, voted on August 25, 1825 for independence from Brazil and union with the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata. The Buenos Aires Congress accepted the incorporation on October 25, which led the Empire to declare war.

hechos/batalla-de-sarandi/resumen.texto: The Eastern forces of Lavalleja and Rivera defeated the Brazilian cavalry near Sarandí Grande on October 12, 1825. The victory affirmed the insurrection in the countryside and led the Buenos Aires Congress to accept the incorporation of the province.

hechos/guerra-del-brasil/resumen.texto: War between the United Provinces and the Empire of Brazil over the Banda Oriental, which Brazil declared in December 1825. The republican army won at Ituzaingó and Brown’s squadron at Juncal, but the Brazilian blockade cut off the Buenos Aires customs revenue and several provinces sent neither men nor resources. It ended in 1828, through British mediation, with the independence of the disputed territory as the Eastern State of Uruguay.

hechos/bloqueo-brasileno-1826-1828/titul.texto: Brazilian Blockade of the Río de la Plata

hechos/bloqueo-brasileno-1826-1828/resum.texto: From December 1825 the Brazilian squadron blockaded Buenos Aires and the coast of the Río de la Plata. Customs revenue, the government’s main resource, fell sharply; the government financed the war with legal tender notes of the National Bank, which depreciated, and prices rose in the city.

hechos/combate-de-los-pozos/resumen.texto: On June 11, 1826 Guillermo Brown’s flotilla repelled, off the coast of Buenos Aires, the attack of a much superior Brazilian fleet, in sight of the city’s population.

hechos/batalla-de-juncal/resumen.texto: On February 8 and 9, 1827, Brown’s squadron destroyed and captured, on the Uruguay River near Juncal Island, the Brazilian naval division operating on that river. It was the main republican naval victory of the war.

hechos/batalla-de-ituzaingo/resumen.texto: On February 20, 1827 the republican army of Carlos María de Alvear defeated the imperial army of the Marquis of Barbacena at the Paso del Rosario, in the territory of Rio Grande do Sul. The Brazilians withdrew in good order, and the victorious army, without horses or resources to continue, could not take advantage of the victory.

hechos/batalla-de-monte-santiago/resumen.texto: Between April 7 and 8, 1827 Brown’s squadron, which was trying to break the blockade, was defeated off the Ensenada de Barragán and lost two of its best ships. After this defeat the blockade was kept until the end of the war.

hechos/rechazo-de-la-convencion-garcia/t.texto: Rejection of the García Convention and Rivadavia’s Resignation

hechos/rechazo-de-la-convencion-garcia/r.texto: Manuel José García returned from Rio de Janeiro in June 1827 with a convention recognizing the Banda Oriental as a Brazilian province. The press and public opinion in Buenos Aires reacted against it, Rivadavia rejected it before Congress and, without support from the provinces or resources to continue the war, resigned the presidency on June 27, 1827.

hechos/campana-de-las-misiones-orientale.texto: Rivera’s Campaign in the Eastern Missions

Between April and May 1828 Fructuoso Rivera occupied with few men the towns of the Eastern Missions, held by Brazil since 1801. The occupation increased pressure on the Empire to negotiate, but in the peace of 1828 the region was left to Brazil.

hechos/convencion-preliminar-de-paz/resu.texto: On August 27, 1828 envoys of Governor Dorrego and Emperor Pedro I signed in Rio de Janeiro, with the mediation of the British Lord Ponsonby, the peace that created an independent state in the Banda Oriental. Ponsonby’s correspondence shows that Great Britain sought a Río de la Plata open to its trade and not dominated by either of the two contenders; the two parties, without resources to continue the war, accepted that solution.

hechos/independencia-del-uruguay/resumen.texto: The Convention of 1828 declared the Eastern Province independent, and its constituent assembly enacted a constitution sworn on July 18, 1830; Rivera was elected the first president. In Uruguay it has been debated since the 19th century whether independence was born of the Eastern will of 1825 or of the British mediation of 1828, and the boundaries between the two countries on the Río de la Plata were not fixed until the treaty of 1973.

hechos/abdicacion-de-pedro-i/titulo.texto: Abdication of Pedro I of Brazil

hechos/abdicacion-de-pedro-i/resumen.texto: Worn down by the loss of the Cisplatine Province, conflicts with the Assembly and the succession crisis in Portugal, Pedro I abdicated on April 7, 1831 in favor of his five-year-old son, Pedro II, and left for Europe. Brazil was governed by regencies until 1840.

hechos/gobierno-de-dorrego/resumen.texto: Elected governor of Buenos Aires in August 1827, Dorrego received from the provinces the handling of foreign relations and the war. With the Treasury empty and the blockade, he accepted British mediation and signed the peace of 1828; his government founded the Fortaleza Protectora Argentina in Bahía Blanca.

hechos/fundacion-de-bahia-blanca/titulo.texto: Founding of the Fortaleza Protectora Argentina (Bahía Blanca)

hechos/fundacion-de-bahia-blanca/resumen.texto: On April 11, 1828 Colonel Ramón Estomba founded, by order of Dorrego’s government, the Fortaleza Protectora Argentina on Bahía Blanca, to advance the frontier with the Indigenous peoples of the south and to have a port south of the Salado. It is the origin of the city of Bahía Blanca.

hechos/motin-del-1-de-diciembre-de-1828/.texto: Troops returning from the war with Brazil, led by Juan Lavalle and supported by Unitarian leaders, overthrew Governor Dorrego. An assembly gathered in the chapel of San Roque elected Lavalle governor, and Dorrego went out to the countryside to gather forces.

hechos/batalla-de-navarro/resumen.texto: On December 9, 1828 Lavalle defeated near Navarro the militias that Dorrego and Rosas had gathered in the countryside. Rosas withdrew toward Santa Fe, and Dorrego was captured by officers of his own forces, who handed him over to Lavalle.

hechos/fusilamiento-de-dorrego/resumen.texto: On December 13, 1828 Lavalle had Dorrego shot at Navarro without trial or war council, and reported it to the delegated government in a note in which he personally assumed responsibility. The letters of Juan Cruz Varela and Salvador María del Carril, known decades later, show that Unitarian civil leaders urged him to do so. The execution united the federalists against Lavalle and opened Rosas’s path; liberal historiography tended to attribute it to the error of a poorly advised military man, and revisionist historiography presents it as a political crime of the entire Unitarian party.

hechos/batalla-de-san-roque/resumen.texto: On April 22, 1829 General José María Paz, who had arrived in Córdoba with a division of the Brazilian army, defeated Governor Juan Bautista Bustos and took control of the province.

hechos/batalla-de-puente-de-marquez/resu.texto: On April 26, 1829 the forces of Estanislao López and Juan Manuel de Rosas defeated Lavalle, who was confined to the city of Buenos Aires while the federalists dominated the countryside.

hechos/pactos-de-canuelas-y-barracas/res.texto: Lavalle and Rosas signed on June 24, 1829 the Pact of Cañuelas, which ended the war in Buenos Aires and provided for elections with a common list. When that agreement failed, the Pact of Barracas (August 24) gave the provisional government to Juan José Viamonte, and in December the restored legislature elected Rosas governor.

hechos/batalla-de-la-tablada/resumen.texto: On June 22 and 23, 1829, Paz defeated Facundo Quiroga near the city of Córdoba, after Quiroga had come to Bustos’s aid. It was Quiroga’s first defeat and secured Paz’s control of Córdoba.

hechos/batalla-de-oncativo/resumen.texto: On February 25, 1830, Paz again defeated Quiroga at Oncativo, also called Laguna Larga. Quiroga took refuge in Buenos Aires, and the federal governments of the interior fell one after another.

hechos/liga-del-interior/resumen.texto: After Oncativo, nine provinces of the interior allied under Paz’s military leadership, and in August 1830 they gave him supreme military power. The League confronted the Litoral provinces united in the Federal Pact and dissolved in 1831, after Paz’s capture and the defeat at La Ciudadela.

hechos/captura-de-paz/resumen.texto: On May 10, 1831, while scouting the ground near El Tío, in eastern Córdoba, General Paz was brought down with bolas by a Santa Fe party and taken prisoner. He spent nearly eight years in prison in Santa Fe and in Luján, and his capture left the Liga del Interior without leadership.

hechos/batalla-de-la-ciudadela/resumen.texto: On November 4, 1831, Quiroga defeated Gregorio Aráoz de Lamadrid, Paz’s successor at the head of the Liga del Interior, on the outskirts of San Miguel de Tucumán. With this battle, all the provinces came under federal governments.

hechos/debate-sobre-la-aduana-y-los-rios.texto: Controversy between Ferré and Roxas y Patrón over the Customs and the Rivers

During the negotiations of the Federal Pact, Pedro Ferré, for Corrientes, called for protecting the country’s production with bans and surcharges on imports, opening the Paraná and Uruguay rivers to direct trade, distributing the revenue of the Buenos Aires customs among all the provinces, and convening a congress. José María Roxas y Patrón, for Buenos Aires, defended free trade and the preservation of the porteño customs, and rejected convening the congress. Corrientes did not sign the pact in January 1831 and adhered in August. Historians see this controversy as the clearest formulation of the conflict between the port and the provinces, and they debate how much it influenced Rosas’s customs law of 1835.

hechos/firma-del-pacto-federal/resumen.texto: Buenos Aires, Santa Fe, and Entre Ríos signed an alliance against the Liga del Interior in Santa Fe on January 4, 1831, and created a Representative Commission charged with convening a federal congress. Corrientes adhered on August 19, 1831, and after the League’s defeat the other provinces joined.

hechos/comision-representativa-1831-1832.texto: The Representative Commission and the Congress That Never Met

The Representative Commission of the Litoral governments, provided for in the Federal Pact, met in Santa Fe in 1831 and 1832. When Corrientes, through Manuel Leiva, and other provinces demanded the convening of the congress under Article 16, Buenos Aires opposed it, withdrew its delegate Roxas y Patrón, and the commission dissolved in 1832. In his letter from the Hacienda de Figueroa (1834), Rosas argued that constitutional organization was premature, and the congress did not meet until 1852, after his fall.

hechos/asesinato-de-quiroga/titulo.texto: Assassination of Facundo Quiroga at Barranca Yaco

hechos/asesinato-de-quiroga/resumen.texto: On February 16, 1835, while returning from a mediation mission in the north commissioned by the Buenos Aires government, Quiroga was ambushed and killed at Barranca Yaco, in northern Córdoba, together with his secretary José Santos Ortiz and nearly his entire retinue, by a party under Captain Santos Pérez. The later trial attributed the order to the Reinafé brothers, who governed Córdoba. Suspicion also fell on Estanislao López, his protector, and Sarmiento hinted in the Facundo at Rosas’s responsibility, but none of these accusations was proven. A few weeks later, on March 7, 1835, the Buenos Aires Legislature elected Rosas governor with full public powers, amid the crisis opened by the crime.

hechos/juicio-a-los-reinafe/titulo.texto: Trial and Execution of the Reinafé Brothers

hechos/juicio-a-los-reinafe/resumen.texto: Rosas had the accused brought to Buenos Aires for trial, although the crime had been committed in Córdoba. After a long process, José Vicente and Guillermo Reinafé, Santos Pérez, and other defendants were executed in the Plaza de la Victoria on October 25, 1837, and their bodies were hanged. José Antonio Reinafé had died in prison, and Francisco escaped. The trial did not clarify whether there were other instigators, which kept suspicions about López and Rosas alive.

hechos/firma-del-protocolo-de-palermo/re.texto: On April 6, 1852, two months after Caseros, Urquiza and the representatives of Buenos Aires, Corrientes, and Santa Fe agreed in Palermo to entrust him with foreign relations and to convene the governors to organize the country.

hechos/reconocimiento-de-la-independenci.texto: On July 17, 1852, Santiago Derqui, Urquiza’s envoy, signed in Asunción with the government of Carlos Antonio López the act by which the Argentine Confederation recognized the independence of Paraguay, which Rosas had refused to recognize.

hechos/firma-del-acuerdo-de-san-nicolas/.texto: The governors gathered by Urquiza in San Nicolás de los Arroyos signed on May 31, 1852 the agreement convening the constituent congress, with two deputies per province, and naming Urquiza provisional director of the Confederation. The provinces were to contribute to national expenses with the revenue from their foreign customs, which in practice meant above all the customs of Buenos Aires.

hechos/jornadas-de-junio-de-1852/resumen.texto: Between June 21 and 23, 1852, the Buenos Aires Legislature debated the Agreement of San Nicolás and, with speeches by Bartolomé Mitre and Dalmacio Vélez Sarsfield, among others, rejected it for the powers it gave Urquiza, the equal representation of the provinces, and the surrender of the customs. Governor Vicente López y Planes resigned, and Urquiza dissolved the Legislature, took over the government of the province, closed opposition newspapers, and exiled several of its leaders.

hechos/revolucion-del-11-de-septiembre-1.texto: While Urquiza was traveling to Santa Fe for the opening of the congress, the city’s troops, under General José María Pirán, rose up with the support of Buenos Aires liberals, reestablished the Legislature, and repudiated the Agreement of San Nicolás. At the end of October the Legislature elected Valentín Alsina governor. Buenos Aires withdrew its deputies and remained separated from the rest of the Confederation.

hechos/sitio-de-buenos-aires-1852-1853/r.texto: In December 1852, Federal colonel Hilario Lagos rose up in the countryside against the porteño government and besieged the city. In 1853 Urquiza joined the siege with troops and with the Confederation’s squadron. In June 1853 the commander of that squadron, John Halstead Coe, handed it over to Buenos Aires in exchange for money, and on July 13 Urquiza lifted the siege.

hechos/congreso-constituyente-de-santa-f.texto: General Constituent Congress of Santa Fe

The congress, with two deputies from each province except Buenos Aires, was installed in Santa Fe on November 20, 1852 under the presidency of Facundo Zuviría. It enacted the Constitution in 1853 and continued to function as the legislative power until the national Congress was installed in 1854.

hechos/sancion-constitucion-1853/resumen.texto: In April 1853 the congress rejected Zuviría’s proposal to postpone the constitution until there was peace with Buenos Aires, and on May 1 it enacted the Constitution. Urquiza promulgated it on May 25, and the provinces swore to it on July 9. The draft, presented by Gorostiaga on behalf of the Constitutional Affairs committee, whose members also included Manuel Leiva, Juan María Gutiérrez, Pedro Díaz Colodrero, and Pedro Ferré, followed mainly the Constitution of the United States and Alberdi’s draft. Buenos Aires did not accept it until the reform of 1860.

hechos/polemica-alberdi-sarmiento/resume.texto: From Chile, Alberdi published the Cartas quillotanas in early 1853 against Sarmiento’s opposition press to Urquiza, and Sarmiento replied with Las ciento y una. The controversy set those who supported the Confederation against those who sided with Buenos Aires within anti-Rosas liberalism.

hechos/libre-navegacion-de-los-rios-1853.texto: Treaties on Free Navigation of the Rivers

Urquiza had decreed free navigation of the rivers for ships of all nations in August and October 1852, and the Constitution incorporated it. On July 10, 1853, the Confederation confirmed it through treaties with Great Britain, France, and the United States, which allowed Rosario, Paraná, Corrientes, and Asunción to trade with the outside world without passing through Buenos Aires.

hechos/secesion-de-buenos-aires/titulo.texto: Separation of the State of Buenos Aires

hechos/secesion-de-buenos-aires/resumen.texto: From the revolution of September 11, 1852 until 1860, Buenos Aires governed itself as a state separate from the Confederation, with its own 1854 constitution, its own currency, and the customs of its port, which handled most of the country’s foreign trade.
